title: Ultrasound-guided nerve blocks in the emergency department: head, chest wall and shoulder
summary: Four blocks which change a patient's emergency department stay: the greater occipital nerve block for headache, the serratus anterior plane block for rib fractures, and the superior trunk and SHAC blocks for the shoulder. Learn the safety system first, then the sonoanatomy, the needle path and the evidence for each block.
author: Dr Firas Abou-Auda, Consultant in Emergency Medicine and Course Director, Wavelength
conflicts: Dr Firas Abou-Auda is Course Director of Wavelength, which runs paid ultrasound courses.
audience: Emergency and acute care doctors and advanced clinical practitioners who perform, or are training to perform, ultrasound-guided regional anaesthesia under their trust's governance.
outcomes: Set up a safe block: consent, dose calculation, monitoring, Stop Before You Block and documentation
Recognise local anaesthetic systemic toxicity early and manage it with lipid emulsion
Perform the sonoanatomy and needle path for the greater occipital nerve, serratus anterior plane, superior trunk and SHAC blocks
Choose between the shoulder blocks, and recognise who should not have each one
Summarise the evidence for each block in emergency care, and its limits
references: Association of Anaesthetists. Management of severe local anaesthetic toxicity. Safety guideline. 2010.
Regional Anaesthesia UK and the Safe Anaesthesia Liaison Group. Stop Before You Block.
